strengths: Provides a principled theoretical bridge between stochastic optimal control (SOC), Tweedie-based training-free guidance, and Stein variational inference, deriving a novel variational upper bound on the SOC value function (Proposition 3.2) that explains why naive Tweedie-based posterior approximation is suboptimal and motivates a KL-correction term.

The proposed 'back-and-forth correction trick' is a clever practical solution to the otherwise intractable Jacobian-vector product computation required for exact Stein correction on the noisy manifold, making the method computationally feasible.

Comprehensive empirical study on a challenging, practically relevant task (structure-based molecular generation across three protein targets) with multiple complementary analyses: novel hit ratio (Table 1), top-5% docking scores (Table 3), docking score distributions (Fig. 3), reward/score dynamics during sampling (Fig. 5, 9, 10), and extreme low-density validity experiments (Fig. 6).

The ablation (SDG vs. SDG w/o Stein correction) directly isolates the contribution of the proposed correction mechanism and shows consistent, sometimes dramatic, improvements, supporting the central theoretical claim.
Detailed appendix with full proofs of the propositions and reasonably thorough reporting of experimental/hyperparameter details (schedules, normalization, hardware), aiding reproducibility.
Good qualitative visualizations (docking poses) that provide some non-quantitative sanity check of generated molecule plausibility.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is confined entirely to one domain (molecular graph generation with GDSS/MOOD backbones); despite claims of broader applicability, no experiments on images or other modalities are provided to substantiate generality claimed in the abstract/conclusion.

The only training-free baseline compared against is the paper's own ablation ('SDG w/o Stein correction'), which is not benchmarked against other established training-free guidance methods from the literature (e.g., FreeDoM, DPS, loss-based guidance variants cited in related work) adapted to the molecular graph setting; this makes it hard to assess whether the reported gains are specific to the authors' own baseline implementation rather than a fair comparison to the broader training-free literature.

No discussion or measurement of the additional computational overhead introduced by the particle-based Stein correction (O(N^2) kernel evaluations per correction step, extra forward/backward Tweedie mappings), despite the paper's original motivation being computational efficiency relative to full SOC simulation; a runtime/complexity comparison against SOC and vanilla training-free guidance is missing.

The back-and-forth correction is itself an approximation (correcting on MT via Tweedie-mapped particles rather than exactly on Mt), and no theoretical or empirical error bound is given for how well this approximates the exact Stein correction described just prior in Section 3.3.

Some reported ablation numbers appear inconsistent or extreme (e.g., 'SDG w/o Stein correction' achieving exactly 0.000±0.000 novel hit ratio on jak2, underperforming even the un-guided GDSS baseline), raising questions about whether the baseline hyperparameters (β, α schedules) were properly tuned for fairness, or whether the comparison is deliberately weakened to highlight the proposed correction.

Results are averaged over only three sampling runs, which is a fairly small number for stochastic generative methods and limits confidence in the statistical robustness of reported improvements, especially where margins are narrow (e.g., fa7 hit ratio where FREED slightly outperforms SDG).

The central motivating hypothesis that high-value/novel molecules reside in low-density regions is asserted but not directly empirically validated; the connection between the annealing parameter α and actual sparsity of true data density is not rigorously demonstrated beyond indirect validity/hit-ratio proxies.

The paper's notation and derivation chain (Propositions 3.1–3.3, cost functionals with Dirac delta state costs) are dense and could be better motivated/explained for readability; some steps (e.g., the physical interpretation of the δ(s-t) state cost, and why this specific cost functional is the 'right' choice for low-density sampling) are not intuitively justified.

Limited discussion of practical failure modes or hyperparameter sensitivity beyond a single table of tuned settings per protein target, making it unclear how robust SDG is to hyperparameter misspecification in new applications.

strengths: The paper provides a coherent theoretical narrative connecting stochastic optimal control, Tweedie-based training-free guidance, and Stein variational inference, culminating in a variational upper bound (Prop. 3.2) that motivates the need for a posterior-correction term beyond the standard Tweedie approximation.

The proposed 'back-and-forth' Stein correction trick to avoid expensive Jacobian-vector products through the diffusion trajectory is a reasonable practical approximation to make the method tractable at inference time.

The ablation comparing SDG to 'SDG w/o Stein correction' isolates the contribution of the proposed correction mechanism and is reported across three distinct protein targets (fa7, 5ht1b, jak2), with additional diagnostic analyses (reward estimation reliability, docking-score distributions, manifold score norms, validity under extreme low-density settings) that attempt to explain why the correction helps.
The extension to permutation-invariant graph diffusion models (node/edge score networks) is a sensible and concrete instantiation of the general framework for molecular graphs.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is limited to a single application domain (molecular docking against three proteins) despite the abstract's and conclusion's claims of 'broader applications' and generality across modalities; no experiments on images or other standard training-free-guidance benchmarks are provided to support generality.

The magnitude of improvement over the strongest existing baseline (MOOD) is inconsistent and sometimes marginal (e.g., fa7: 1.011 vs. 0.733; jak2: 9.367 vs. 9.200), which does not strongly support the claim that SDG 'significantly outperforms' training-free guidance methods; only the 5ht1b result shows a large gap, and no statistical significance testing is reported despite standard deviations being given.

The ablation baseline ('SDG w/o Stein correction') performs far worse than even the unguided/weakly-guided GDSS baseline (e.g., 0.000% on jak2), which is an unusually poor result for a 'standard training-free guidance' baseline and raises concern that this ablation may be under-tuned or not representative of properly implemented Tweedie-based training-free guidance methods from the literature (e.g., FreeDoM, DPS), making the central comparison supporting the paper's main claim look potentially cherry-picked.

No wall-clock time or computational cost comparison is provided between SDG, its ablation, and the baselines, despite the paper's central motivation being computational efficiency relative to full SOC simulation; it remains unclear whether the Stein correction's added overhead (pairwise kernel evaluations across a particle batch at every reverse step) is actually cheap in practice.

The per-target hyperparameter tables (Appendix C.6.1) show that annealing schedules, SNR values, and max guidance strengths are individually tuned for each of the three protein targets, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns and suggesting the strong numbers may partly reflect target-specific tuning rather than a robust general-purpose method.

The Stein correction in Algorithm 1 appears to use only a single particle-update step at each diffusion timestep; the paper does not empirically verify how close the resulting q_T|t actually gets to the true posterior p_T|t, so the central theoretical motivation (minimizing KL to the true posterior) is not directly validated, only inferred from downstream task performance.

The core assumption that high-value molecules lie predominantly in low-density regions of the pretrained generative model is asserted as a hypothesis rather than empirically or theoretically justified, which undercuts the motivation for the entire low-density guidance framework.

The theoretical contribution (Prop. 3.2) is a relatively standard ELBO/Jensen's-inequality argument combined with known SVGD machinery (Liu & Wang) and existing SOC-to-classifier-guidance connections (Uehara et al.); the novelty is primarily in combining established pieces rather than a fundamentally new theoretical insight, which should be reflected in tempered significance claims.

Figure 6 shows that under more extreme low-density settings, molecular validity degrades substantially even with Stein correction (e.g., ~40% at α_E=0.7), suggesting the method's robustness claims are limited to moderate low-density regimes and may not hold in the most extreme (and arguably most scientifically interesting) sparse regions the paper motivates the work around.

strengths: Clear theoretical development: the paper derives a novel SOC cost functional for low-density guidance (Prop 3.1), a variational upper bound on the value function (Prop 3.2) that explicitly reveals the KL-regularization term missing in standard Tweedie-based training-free guidance, and an optimal controller decomposition (Prop 3.3) that operationalizes this bound via a Stein correction plus guidance step. The logic connecting SOC, Tweedie's formula, and SVGD is coherent and proofs are provided in the appendix.

The 'back-and-forth correction trick' is a practical and reasonably well-motivated solution to the computational burden of evaluating Jacobian-vector products for Stein corrections on the noisy manifold, mapping the problem to the clean manifold instead.

Strong and consistent empirical gains over the relevant baselines (GDSS, MOOD) and several non-diffusion baselines across three distinct protein targets, with especially large improvements on 5ht1b (18.7% to 25.7% novel hit ratio) and jak2.

The ablation removing the Stein correction is convincing and informative: it shows the correction is not a minor refinement but essential, with performance collapsing (e.g., 0% hit ratio on jak2) without it, directly supporting the central theoretical claim.

Additional diagnostic experiments (Section 4.3, 4.4) analyzing reward overestimation, off-manifold drift of score norms, and validity under extreme low-density settings provide good mechanistic insight into why the correction helps, beyond just aggregate metrics.
Reasonably thorough appendix with hyperparameters, compute details, and extensive additional visualizations (docking poses, per-protein radar plots, sampling dynamics) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined entirely to molecular/graph generation; despite claims of broad applicability to 'conditional sampling... across various domains,' no experiments on images or other modalities are provided, and this is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation in one sentence.

No computational cost/runtime comparison is reported between SDG, SDG w/o Stein correction, MOOD, and SOC-based fine-tuning baselines, despite the paper's framing around computational efficiency relative to full SOC simulation; the SVGD-based back-and-forth correction with N particles and kernel evaluations at every diffusion step plausibly adds non-trivial overhead that is never quantified.

The method requires per-protein tuning of several schedules and hyperparameters (snr, α scheduling type, α_max, β_max in Table 2), with no sensitivity analysis showing robustness to these choices or guidance for how to set them on a new target without extensive search.

The paper compares only against a single ablation (no Stein correction) and does not empirically benchmark against other training-free posterior-correction approaches cited in related work (e.g., DPS, FreeDoM, mixture-based/midpoint guidance), making it hard to assess whether the specific Stein-based correction is better than simpler alternative corrections.

The specific cost functional form in Proposition 3.1 (particularly the δ(s−t) term and the choice of log p_t(x) as the density-annealing penalty) is introduced somewhat by assertion rather than being derived from first principles or compared against alternative formulations.

Results are based on only 3 sampling runs per configuration; while standard deviations are reported, this is a relatively small number of trials for stochastic generative sampling, especially given molecule generation's inherent variance.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and compressed derivations in the main text, which may hinder accessibility for readers less familiar with SOC/Feynman-Kac/Stein variational inference machinery.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent theoretical narrative connecting stochastic optimal control (SOC) and Stein variational inference for training-free diffusion guidance: it derives a novel low-density annealing cost functional (Prop. 3.1), a variational upper bound on the SOC value function that exposes a missing KL-regularization term in standard Tweedie-based training-free guidance (Prop. 3.2), and a tractable 'back-and-forth' Stein correction that avoids expensive Jacobian-vector products (Prop. 3.4). The Langevin-correction-as-special-case result (Corollary 3.5) is a nice unifying observation that situates the method relative to prior score-based sampling corrections.

Empirical evaluation spans two fairly different domains (molecular graph generation for ligand-protein binding across three targets, and general image guidance tasks: label guidance, deblurring, super-resolution), which supports a claim of generality beyond the primary molecular use case.

On the molecular low-density sampling task, the reported gains from adding Stein correction are large (often several-fold to orders-of-magnitude improvements in novel hit ratio over the no-correction ablation and over established baselines such as MOOD, GDSS, FREED, HierVAE, MORLD), and the paper backs this up with multiple complementary diagnostics (docking score distributions, FCD/NSPDK distributional distances, validity under increasing OOD levels, reward-overestimation analysis, temporal score dynamics).

The appendix is unusually thorough: full proofs, algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, computational cost breakdowns (runtime/memory), and docking pose visualizations, which aids reproducibility and transparency about design choices (e.g., adaptive step size, annealing schedules, Polyak guidance-strength step).
weaknesses: The central motivating claim -- that SDG is a cheaper but still faithful alternative to full SOC-based guidance -- is never empirically validated against an actual SOC baseline (e.g., Uehara et al. 2024's entropy-regularized control or Domingo-Enrich et al.'s SOC matching) on the molecular or image tasks; only asymptotic complexity (O(T) vs O(T^2)) is compared (Appendix C.3.6), leaving the core accuracy-cost trade-off unverified experimentally.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly positive: in Table 1 (label guidance), adding the Stein correction improves classification accuracy but visibly worsens FID relative to the no-correction ablation (89.50 to 105.4), a trade-off the paper acknowledges but does not analyze further or reconcile with the theoretical claim that Stein correction keeps samples 'within the manifold'.

The method introduces a substantial computational overhead (runtime roughly doubles per Tables 6-7) and a large number of additional hyperparameters (snr, particle count N, α/β schedules and maxima, correction step size ε(t)), with an explicitly reported hyperparameter search grid; combined with Table 3's non-monotonic/inconsistent behavior as particle count increases (e.g., jak2 hit ratio decreasing from 512 to 1024 particles before rising again at 3000), this raises concerns about the practical robustness and tuning burden of the proposed correction in new settings.

Molecular baselines used for comparison (HierVAE 2020, MORLD 2020, FREED 2021, GDSS 2022, MOOD 2023) are relatively dated; more recent training-free guidance methods cited in the related work (e.g., MOUFAD, Rout et al. 2025, Janati et al. 2025, Dinh et al. 2025) are not empirically benchmarked on the molecular task, so the comparison to contemporary training-free alternatives is incomplete outside the image experiments.

Evaluation of binding affinity relies entirely on a docking-score proxy (QuickVina2) rather than any independent validation, and the paper does not discuss error or bias in this reward model beyond the general 'reward overestimation' discussion, which somewhat limits the strength of claims about discovering genuinely higher-affinity molecules.

Presentation is dense, with heavy notation overload (e.g., closely related symbols for annealing schedule, guidance strength, and correction step size) that could benefit from a consolidated notation table or more intuitive exposition, particularly for readers less versed in SOC/Stein variational inference.

strengths: The paper offers an interesting theoretical lens connecting training-free diffusion guidance (Tweedie-based), stochastic optimal control, and Stein variational inference: Proposition 3.2's variational upper bound cleanly shows that standard Tweedie-based guidance omits a KL regularization term, motivating the proposed correction in a principled way.

The 'back-and-forth' Stein correction is a reasonably elegant engineering trick that avoids expensive Jacobian-vector products required by naive SVGD on high-dimensional diffusion states, and the derivation that it generalizes Song et al.'s Langevin corrector (Corollary 3.5) is a nice unifying observation.

The experimental scope is fairly broad, spanning both general image guidance tasks (label guidance, deblurring, super-resolution) and molecular binding-affinity guidance across three protein targets, with multiple ablations (density level, particle count, annealing schedule, computational cost).

The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations, explicitly reporting the ~2x runtime overhead of the Stein correction (Table 6/7) and the lack of consistent benefit from increasing particle count (Table 3), rather than hiding these less favorable results.
weaknesses: The core empirical validation largely compares SDG against its own ablation ('SDG w/o Stein correction') rather than against strong, recent training-free guidance baselines referenced in the introduction (e.g., FreeDoM, MPGD, MOUFAD, Rout et al., Janati et al.); in the molecular task the only non-ablation baselines are older non-diffusion methods (HierVAE, MORLD, FREED) and GDSS/MOOD, leaving the central claim of superiority over contemporary training-free guidance methods largely untested.

The theoretical chain itself relies on several uncontrolled approximations stacked on top of each other: Lemma 3.3's derivation uses a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate and then further drops a non-negligible term (Eq. 16) to arrive at the posterior-score approximation used for the 'exact' Stein direction; no bound is given on the resulting approximation error, which undercuts the paper's own critique that Tweedie-based approximations are 'biased and unreliable.'

Table 3 shows that increasing the number of SVGD particles does not consistently improve (and sometimes worsens) performance, which is inconsistent with the paper's theoretical motivation that more particles better approximate the true posterior; this raises doubts about the practical reliability of the proposed correction and is only superficially explained by citing instability of high-dimensional SVGD.

The reported computational overhead is substantial (roughly 1.85–2x runtime, Tables 6–7), which weakens the claimed advantage of being a 'low-cost' alternative to full SOC, especially since the per-step Stein correction requires pairwise particle interactions that can scale poorly with particle count N.

Statistical reporting is thin: results are averaged over only 3 runs with suspiciously small standard deviations for a stochastic molecular generation pipeline (e.g., Table 2), and no significance testing is provided to support claims of 'consistent' and 'substantial' improvement.

In the general image guidance task (Table 1), SDG's gains are mixed rather than clearly superior: it improves classification accuracy in label guidance but at a notably worse FID (105.4 vs. 89.5 for the ablation), undermining the claim of consistent improvement and suggesting a trade-off rather than a strict win.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and multiple overloaded symbols (e.g., overloaded use of forward/backward terminology, many schedules α(t), β(t), ε(t)), which makes it difficult to independently verify the full pipeline (Algorithm 1) without careful cross-referencing across the main text and appendix.

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical bridge between expensive SOC-based diffusion guidance and cheap Tweedie-based training-free guidance, formalizing the latter as a biased approximation via a clean variational (Jensen) upper bound on the SOC value function (Props 3.1–3.4), which cleanly explains why existing training-free guidance methods are suboptimal (missing KL-correction term).

Introduces a practical 'back-and-forth' Stein correction that avoids expensive Jacobian-vector product computations required by naive SVGD on the data manifold, and shows it provably reduces to the well-known Langevin corrector as a special case (Corollary 3.5), nicely unifying prior heuristics under one framework.

Strong, consistent empirical gains on the core low-density molecular sampling task across three protein targets (fa7, 5ht1b, jak2), with orders-of-magnitude improvement in novel hit ratio over both diffusion and non-diffusion baselines (HierVAE, MORLD, FREED, GDSS, MOOD) and over the ablation without Stein correction.

Extensive ablation studies (particle count, annealing schedule type, extreme low-density/OOD levels, computational cost) and a reasonably thorough appendix with full proofs, hyperparameters, docking pose visualizations, and sampling-dynamics diagnostics that support the paper's qualitative claims (e.g., reward overestimation, off-manifold drift).

Demonstrates the method's generality by also testing on standard (non-low-density) image guidance tasks (label guidance, deblurring, super-resolution), showing the Stein correction helps beyond the molecular domain, and provides a computational complexity argument (O(T) vs O(T^2) for full SOC) with measured runtime/memory overhead.
weaknesses: Reported standard deviations in the main hit-ratio results (Table 2) are large relative to the means and are computed over only 3 runs, raising concerns about the statistical reliability of the headline 'order of magnitude' improvement claims, especially for metrics near zero.

The core theoretical guarantee is a possibly loose variational upper bound obtained via Jensen's inequality; the paper does not quantify or empirically bound the tightness of this surrogate objective, so improvements in the bound are not rigorously shown to track improvements in the true value function/posterior fidelity beyond qualitative visualization (Figure 1).

The method stacks several approximations (Tweedie posterior-mean estimate, one-sample Monte Carlo score identity in Lemma 3.3, Gaussian forward-kernel assumption, finite-particle SVGD), and acknowledged limitations (Table 3, Section 4.2.3) show that increasing particle count does not monotonically improve results, pointing to unresolved instability inherited from standard SVGD in high dimensions.

Image-domain evaluation (Table 1) is compared against only two baselines (DPS, LGD) rather than the broader modern training-free guidance literature, limiting the strength of the generalizability claim; accuracy gains also come with higher FID in the label-guidance setting, an unaddressed trade-off.

Reliance on docking scores (QuickVina2) as the binding-affinity oracle is a common but imperfect proxy with no wet-lab or higher-fidelity computational validation, so claims about 'discovery of molecules with higher binding affinities' should be read as in-silico only.

Practical overhead is non-trivial (~2x runtime, increased memory per Tables 6–7) relative to standard training-free guidance, and no code release is mentioned, which combined with the dense, heavily overloaded notation (α, β, ε, η, γ, σ schedules) may hinder independent reproducibility.
